# VaultScaler

> VaultScaler is private, on-premise computer-vision security — proven first on a working artist's own collection, and built for private collectors, galleries, museums, and other discreet, privacy-sensitive spaces. It designs, specifies, and configures the system. The system watches the whole space — including the people in it — and the owner decides what it remembers: recognise known people and flag unknowns, or obscure every face before anything is ever stored. The intelligence runs on hardware the customer owns, in their building; nothing it sees ever leaves the building, and nothing is ever attached to what it protects. Bespoke and consulting-led — designed and configured by VaultScaler, installed by a licensed contractor. Based in Las Vegas. Founded in 2025.

VaultScaler's approach has three parts. At the edge: the system runs on a box in the customer's building — no cloud, no account, nothing phoned home. There is no server for anyone to subpoena, breach, or browse, because there isn't a server. Honest by design: the system knows the difference between someone pausing to look and something actually being taken — so it does not cry wolf, and the alarms mean something. Owned end to end: VaultScaler builds and trains its own computer vision on its own hardware; the intelligence is theirs, not rented from a platform that can change its terms or cut them off.

## The three problems VaultScaler exists to fix

1. Cloud camera systems put a space's footage, the people who trust it, and what happens inside its walls on infrastructure the owner does not control — viewable by strangers and reachable by anyone who breaches it. For anyone whose business depends on discretion, that is the risk, not a feature.
2. Conventional motion and object sensors cannot tell someone pausing to look from something actually being taken. The false alarms are constant, so most systems get quietly disconnected. A system nobody trusts is a system nobody uses.
3. Sometimes the hardware touches the thing itself. In a gallery, that's tags behind canvases, laser curtains, contacts and vibration sensors on the frame — it works, but it touches the piece, constrains how it's shown, and announces itself to every visitor. The same problem shows up anywhere something valuable can't be wired without the wiring diminishing it.

## What the system does

- Nothing leaves the building: intelligence runs on owned hardware on-premise; no cloud, no account, nothing phoned home — as an architecture, not a policy.
- It knows the difference: it understands a person in front of a work versus a work that is gone. Admiring the work does not trigger an alarm; removing it does. This distinction is the hardest problem in the field and the one built for first.
- Nothing touches the artwork: the camera watches; the work hangs unwired, untagged, unconstrained. Rehang the room whenever you like and the system is re-taught in minutes.
- Fewer guards, better cover: it watches every piece at once, without breaks; it does not replace staff but means fewer are needed, and they know exactly where to go.

## What it sees

- Every work, individually — draw a boundary around each piece; the system learns what that wall looks like with the work on it.
- Removal — if a work leaves its place, you know within seconds.
- Contact — if someone reaches into a piece, you know immediately.
- People — recognise staff, regulars, and collectors and flag unknown people; or run fully anonymous with every face obscured before it is ever stored. The owner's building, rules, and call.
- A record you can use — every event, timestamped, with an image: who was where, when, and what they touched.
- Open hours and closed hours — the system knows a busy opening from an empty room at 3am and behaves accordingly.

## How VaultScaler works (a consultancy, not a shipment)

1. Come and look — walk the room; assess the light, flow, hang, and what is actually at risk.
2. Design for the room — a system specified for the building and collection, not a package.
3. Build it — the computer vision is built and trained by VaultScaler on its own hardware.
4. A licensed contractor installs it — VaultScaler specifies exactly what goes in and where; installation and physical work is carried out by a licensed contractor, then VaultScaler tunes it in person until the false alarms are gone and the system reports only what matters.
5. It's yours — the customer owns the hardware and the footage; no mandatory subscription; it keeps working with no further contact.

## Who it's for

Commercial galleries, private collections, private residences with something worth protecting, artist-run and independent spaces, small museums and institutions — anyone whose business depends on discretion.

## Where VaultScaler is

Based in Las Vegas, where the founder's own studio runs the same system described here — VaultScaler's first live deployment, protecting the founder's own paintings. The architecture is the same everywhere (local, owned, nothing leaving the building), configured to the law of each jurisdiction — the highest security available within the customer's legal framework.
